title: Indonesia's poverty reduction leaves a large economic-security layer exposed to low-productivity work, care constraints, weak mobility, and climate shocks
source_unit: World Bank, Indonesia Poverty Assessment: Pathways Towards Economic Security, released May 2023
geography: Indonesia; national poverty, labor, care, urbanization, human-capital, climate-shock, and fiscal-capacity systems

denominator.unit: Indonesian population under the report's poverty and economic-security framework

extreme_poverty.unit: percent of the population below the report's 2011 PPP extreme-poverty line in 2022

economic_insecurity.value: about one-third of Indonesians remain susceptible to falling into poverty after a shock

shock_set.value: COVID-19, natural disasters, and climate-related events can push economically insecure households into poverty

observations.method: World Bank poverty assessment using poverty and inequality trends, household and labor evidence, sector analysis, fiscal-incidence work, and policy synthesis.
observations.uncertainty: The economic-insecurity share depends on thresholds, survey data, prices, and the report's vulnerability framework; it does not predict which particular household will fall after a given shock or measure multidimensional deprivation.
observations.subgroup: Poor and economically insecure households, with differences by rural and urban location, region, work type, gender, human capital, and disaster exposure.
observations.counterinterpretation: The large decline in extreme poverty is a substantive achievement; exposure above the extreme-poverty line identifies a policy frontier rather than negating earlier gains.

denominator.unit: Indonesian workers and sectoral employment structure described by the assessment

low_value_work.value: Agriculture and low-value-added services drove much poverty reduction, but work was often informal, low-productivity, or insufficient to reach economic security

high_skill_jobs.value: High-skilled jobs remained scarce, limiting pathways to higher earnings

urban_migration.value: Low urban migration limited the number of workers able to benefit from agglomeration and higher-productivity urban opportunities

service_productivity.value: Average service-productivity growth fell from 4.0% in 2000–2013 to 1.7% in 2014–2019 as low-value services expanded faster than high-value services

observations.method: World Bank sectoral, labor-market, urbanization, and productivity analysis; the report distinguishes employment presence from sufficient earnings and productivity.
observations.uncertainty: Sector averages and migration patterns do not identify each worker's feasible alternative, travel or housing cost, skill acquisition, bargaining power, or realized income trajectory; reported associations are not a causal estimate of one mobility policy.
observations.subgroup: Agricultural workers, low-value service workers, urban and rural households, workers without high skills, and people facing housing, congestion, or air-pollution barriers to urban opportunity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low-value services can provide accessible entry and income during structural transition, and staying in a rural area can reflect valued ties or rational choices rather than a simple failure of mobility.

denominator.unit: Indonesian working-age population and household care system

female_labor_force.value: about 50% of women were employed or looking for work, compared with more than 80% of men

care_constraint.value: Home-care responsibilities and cultural norms constrained women's labor-force participation and household livelihood options

gender_pay.value: Women earned less than men, with the report identifying a specific female effect beyond observable characteristics

policy_route.value: Improved quality and affordability of childcare, skills, digital opportunities, and labor-market policy could widen household economic pathways

observations.method: World Bank gender, labor, household-care, and poverty analysis within the national assessment.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies linked constraints but does not provide an individual care episode, childcare take-up, employer response, wage offer, or causal estimate for a particular childcare or digital intervention.
observations.subgroup: Women, mothers and other caregivers, households with dependents, workers facing gender discrimination, and households near poverty or economic-security thresholds.
observations.counterinterpretation: Care work can be a valued household choice and labor-force participation is not the sole measure of welfare; expanding paid work without care quality, autonomy, or safety could shift rather than solve burdens.

observations.period: 1990–2021; climate and disaster exposure as economic-security risk

climate_share.unit: approximate share of disasters attributed to climate-related events in the report's 1990–2021 context

people_affected.value: more than 11 million people affected across more than 300 recorded natural disasters

protection_bundle.value: Social assistance, social insurance, financial inclusion, and resilient infrastructure are presented as complementary buffers against poverty and shocks

fiscal_capacity.value: Higher tax revenue, removal of inefficient subsidies, and stronger subnational administrative capacity are identified as ways to finance pro-poor investment and improve services

observations.method: World Bank disaster, household-resilience, social-protection, financial-inclusion, infrastructure, and fiscal-policy synthesis.
observations.uncertainty: Historical disaster counts and affected-person totals do not establish household loss, aid receipt, rebuilding, displacement, or recovery; recommended protection bundles are not implementation evidence.
observations.subgroup: Disaster-exposed households, poor and near-poor communities, rural and coastal areas, women and caregivers, local governments, and users of social protection and public infrastructure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Informal support, remittances, private adaptation, and local institutions may buffer shocks even where formal protection is thin; resilient infrastructure can also create costs or unequal benefits if allocation is not participatory.

related_sources.claim: World Bank summary explains the report's economic-security threshold, work, shock, and policy pathways.
Official executive summary provides the report's methods, sector, gender, and economic-security findings.

boundary: This comparative record adds a country-level route from poverty reduction through job quality, urban mobility, unpaid care, gendered labor, climate shocks, social protection, infrastructure, and fiscal capacity. It does not infer individual household trajectories, causal effects of a named intervention, service receipt, political response, or durable recovery.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank publication page, executive summary, full report, and summary article reviewed for poverty reduction, economic insecurity, work structure, urban migration, female labor-force participation, care constraints, disaster exposure, protection, and fiscal-capacity pathways.
